content:
Yesterday we saw the great comfort of Numbers 15, that God provided atonement even for the sin done in ignorance, and that the blood of Christ cleanses us from all sin, even the faults we did not know. But Numbers 15:30 suddenly changes the picture, and now Yahweh speaks about someone who sins defiantly, with a high hand. This person is not saying, "Father, I did not understand." He knows. He has heard God's Word. His conscience has warned him. He understands clearly that the action is against God's command, and yet he deliberately chooses it and continues in it. Today we must look honestly at this second kind of sin, for it carries a very solemn warning for the New Creation.

Let us consider some practical examples, so that we understand what this means. God tells us plainly to forgive, but we say, "I know what Scripture says, but I will not forgive." We know that something is dishonest, yet we deliberately continue in it because it benefits us. We know that a certain relationship or practice is drawing us into sin, yet we decide, "I will continue anyway." We know our eyes are looking at something impure, but instead of fleeing from it, we deliberately return to it again and again. We know our words are destroying another person, yet we keep speaking because anger feels more satisfying to us than obedience. James gives a very simple definition of this, "To him who knows to do good and does not do it, to him it is sin" (James 4:17). This is the sin of the lifted hand, knowing what God commands and knowingly refusing it, holding bitterness when we are commanded to forgive, choosing what is false, neglecting what God has told us to do, and knowingly giving ourselves to the very things He has forbidden.

This brings us to the frightening warning in the letter to the Hebrews. "If we sin willfully after we have received the knowledge of the truth..." (Hebrews 10:26). And then the writer describes such hardened rebellion in terrible language.

He speaks of the one "who has trampled the Son of God underfoot, counted the blood of the covenant by which he was sanctified a common thing, and insulted the Spirit of grace" (Hebrews 10:29). Notice that expression carefully, "trampled the Son of God underfoot." This is much stronger than merely stamping something beneath our feet by accident. Hebrews says that hardened, willful rejection actually amounts to trampling the Son of God underfoot, and treating His covenant blood as though it were a common, ordinary thing.

Imagine what this truly means. Christ suffered for sin. His body was broken. His blood was shed. The sinless One became our Sin Offering. And then a person looks at the very sin for which Christ suffered and so terribly bled, and knowingly chooses to embrace it, making peace with it and refusing to repent of it. By his very actions he is saying, "I know what this sin cost Christ, but I choose it anyway." That is why deliberate, hardened sin is so fearful. It is not weakness stumbling in the dark. It is a heart looking straight at the cross, understanding what it cost, and trampling on it. To sin in ignorance is to stumble; to sin with a high hand, knowing the price that was paid, is to despise the very blood that would have washed us.

But here we must make a very important qualification, so that no tender heart is wounded by these words. This warning is not describing a believer who falls into sin, is broken over it, repents, and seeks cleansing. It is describing a heart that is becoming hardened and careless, making peace with sin, and treating Christ's blood as though it were something common. Think of Peter. He denied Christ three times, yet he went out and wept bitterly, and he returned. Think of David. He committed terrible sin, yet when he was confronted, he confessed at once. The difference is not that faithful believers never fall, for they do. The real question is this: what does our heart do when God exposes our sin? Do we tremble and repent? Or do we say, "I know, but I will continue"? It is that second attitude that should frighten us. The one who falls and grieves and returns finds mercy waiting. The one who knows and defies and hardens is the one Numbers 15 and Hebrews 10 warn so solemnly.

The letter to the Hebrews continues, "For we know Him who said, 'Vengeance is Mine, I will repay,' says Yahweh... It is a fearful thing to fall into the hands of the living God" (Hebrews 10:30-31). Grace must therefore never become a permission to rebel. The sacrifice of Christ is complete, and we cannot add another sacrifice to it, for His one offering is fully sufficient and His blood cleanses from all sin. But the very preciousness of that sacrifice is exactly why we must never treat it cheaply. The blood that gives us confidence should also produce in us a deep reverence. The cross that assures us of mercy should also make us hate the very sin that placed our Saviour there. So the New Creation should remain quick to repent and quick to seek cleansing, so that sin never has the opportunity to harden the heart.

So let us hold both halves of this lesson together. When we discover a sin we did not recognize, we need not run away from God. We have a perfect Sin Offering in Christ. We come into the light, we confess it, we receive cleansing, and we change the course of our walk. But when God has clearly shown us that something is sinful, let us never harden our hearts and deliberately continue in it. There is a fearful difference between falling and repenting, and knowing God's will yet defiantly choosing rebellion. May we never trample the Son of God underfoot, or treat the blood of His covenant as a common thing. The blood of Christ is unspeakably precious. Let us live as people who truly know what our cleansing cost, holding the mercy of God with confidence in one hand and holy reverence in the other.

title: Prayer
text:
O Yahweh, holy and gracious God, whose Son shed His blood to make us clean,
Keep us from ever lifting a defiant hand against the truth we know to be Yours.

Let us never make peace with a sin for which our Saviour so dearly suffered.

When You expose our sin, make us like Peter and David, quick to weep and quick to return.

Never let grace become permission, nor let Your precious blood be treated as common.

Give us confidence in Your mercy and deep reverence for the sacrifice of your Son, our Lord Jesus Christ.

"Let us come boldly to the throne of grace, that we may obtain mercy and find grace to help." - Hebrews 4:16

In Christ name, whose blood is precious, we pray. Amen.
